entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14529"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.13.1-Luke.13.9">Lu 13:1-9</reference>. The Lesson, "REPENT OR Perish," Suggested by Two Recent Incidents, and Illustrated by the Parable of the Barren Fig Tree.</title> <div sID="gen28104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14529"/><hi type="bold">1-3. Galileans--</hi>possibly the followers of Judas of Galilee, who, some twenty years before this, taught that Jews should not pay tribute to the Romans, and of whom we learn, from <reference osisRef="Acts.5.37">Ac 5:37</reference>, that he drew after him a multitude of followers, who on his being slain were all dispersed. About this time that party would be at its height, and if Pilate caused this detachment of them to be waylaid and put to death as they were offering their sacrifices at one of the festivals, that would be "mingling their blood with their sacrifices" [Grotius, Webster and Wilkinson, but doubted by De Wette, Meyer, Alford, &c.]. News of this being brought to our Lord, to draw out His views of such, and whether it was not a judgment of Heaven, He simply points them to the practical view of the matter: "These men are not signal examples of divine vengeance, as ye suppose; but every impenitent sinner--ye yourselves, except ye repent--shall be like monuments of the judgment of Heaven, and in a more awful sense." The reference here to the impending destruction of Jerusalem is far from exhausting our Lord's weighty words; they manifestly point to a "perdition" of a more awful kind--future, personal, remediless. <div eID="gen28104" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14540"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.13.18-Luke.13.30">Lu 13:18-30</reference>. Miscellaneous Teachings.</title> <div sID="gen28124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14540"/><hi type="bold">18-21. mustard seed ... leaven--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.30-Mark.4.32">Mr 4:30-32</reference>). The parable of "the Leaven" sets forth, perhaps, rather the inward growth of the kingdom, while "the Mustard Seed" seems to point chiefly to the outward. It being a woman's work to knead, it seems a refinement to say that "the woman" here represents the Church, as the instrument of depositing the leaven. Nor does it yield much satisfaction to understand the "three measures of meal" of that threefold division of our nature into "spirit, soul, and body," (alluded to in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>) or of the threefold partition of the world among the three sons of Noah (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.32">Ge 10:32</reference>), as some do. It yields more real satisfaction to see in this brief parable just the all-penetrating and assimilating quality of the Gospel, by virtue of which it will yet mould all institutions and tribes of men, and exhibit over the whole earth one "Kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ." (See on <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen28124" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14547"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.13.31-Luke.13.35">Lu 13:31-35</reference>. Message to Herod.</title> <div sID="gen28138" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14547"/><hi type="bold">31. and depart hence--</hi>and "go forward," push on. He was on His way out of Perea, east of Jordan, and in Herod's dominions, "journeying towards Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.22">Lu 13:22</reference>). Haunted by guilty fears, probably, Herod wanted to get rid of Him (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14">Mr 6:14</reference>), and seems, from our Lord's answer, to have sent these Pharisees, under pretense of a friendly hint, to persuade Him that the sooner He got beyond Herod's jurisdiction the better it would be for His own safety. Our Lord saw through both of them, and sends the cunning ruler a message couched in dignified and befitting irony. <div eID="gen28138" type="x-p"/>

Haunted by guilty fears, probably, Herod wanted to get rid of Him (see on Mr 6:14 ), and seems, from our Lord's answer, to have sent these Pharisees, under pretense of a friendly hint, to persuade Him that the sooner He got beyond Herod's jurisdiction the better it would be for His own safety. Our Lord saw through both of them, and sends the cunning ruler a message couched in dignified and befitting irony.
